# Pronouncing Meru: a guide for the curious

Saying **Meru** aloud requires more than reading ​Latin letters on a screen. The conventional spelling is only the entry point into a reconstructed sound and a much older tradition. This post unpacks that sound, the Devanagari ‌evidence, the kindred forms, and the mythological record, then shows how the temple preserves the whole argument without pretending that a diacritic was ever lost.

## At a Glance

- **Restored ‌name:** Meru
- **ASCII form:** meru
- **Meaning:** "Name of a fabulous mountain — the central point of Jambūdvīpa, round which the sun, moon and planets revolve; the Olympus of ​Hindu mythology and abode of the gods."
- **Domain of influence:** Cosmic Mountain, Axis Mundi
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** मेरु (Devanagari)

## Overview

**Meru** (*meru*) — The Axis ​Mountain, Olympus of the Hindus · Name of a fabulous mountain — the central point of Jambūdvīpa, round which the sun, moon and planets revolve — belongs to the ​Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Cosmic Mountain, Axis Mundi". The name means "Name of a fabulous mountain — the central point of Jambūdvīpa, round which ​the sun, moon and planets revolve; the Olympus of Hindu mythology and abode of the gods.".

**Meru** is the world’s axle: the golden mountain at the centre of the ​cosmos, around which the sun, moon, and planets revolve, on whose summit Indra’s city stands, and whose four faces of gold, crystal, ruby, and lapis feed the four great ‌rivers of the directions. Every Indian cosmology — Hindu, Buddhist, Jain — puts Meru in the middle; every mandala is its plan.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari ‌as **मेरु**. Etymologically it means "Name of a fabulous mountain — the central point of Jambūdvīpa, round which the sun, moon and planets revolve; the Olympus of Hindu mythology ​and abode of the gods.".

The canonical spelling **Meru** matches the conventional scholarly romanization. The plain ASCII form *meru* contains the same letters, so no lost diacritics or encoding ‌transition is claimed. The name is preserved in Devanagari as **मेरु**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Meru*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Meru ​is written in Devanagari as मेरु
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark ​retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈmɛruː/** — Sanskrit (IAST: Meru).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Me-** — Short e as in “set”; ​the name is pre-Vedic in feel, its etymology uncertain.
- **-ru** — Long ū as in “rule”; the name closes on the resonant liquid.
- **** — The axis mountain — ​the Olympus of Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain cosmology alike.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “MEH-roo”

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Buddhist** — Sumeru — ​“excellent Meru”, the abode of the thirty-three gods
- **Jain** — Meru as the central peak of the middle world

All three Indian religions share Meru — the one ‌mountain in the centre of every map.

## Mythology

Meru’s mythology is cosmography — the mountain’s biography is the world’s architecture. It rises from the centre of Jambudvīpa, the rose-apple ​continent; the sun’s chariot circles it daily; the Ganges falls first on its summit and only then to the earth; and the gods’ wars are fought on its terraces. ‌The Purāṇic geographies measure all distance from its base.

### The Mountain of Measure (Purāṇic Cosmography)

The Purāṇas give Meru its statistics: 84,000 leagues high, its base 32,000 across, its ​summit the square of the gods’ city. The sun’s horses, tired from circling it, rest at night on its western face; the moon’s waxing is the gods’ drinking of ‌the lunar soma on its terraces. The mountain is the cosmos’s clock, scale, and sceptre.

### The River’s First Fall (Gangā Cycle)

When Bhagīratha won the Ganges’ descent for ​his burned ancestors, the river fell first from heaven onto the matted hair of Śiva — and before that, the tradition adds, upon Meru’s summit, where the gods’ gardens ‌divided her into the seven streams. Meru is the river’s first landing, heaven’s customs-house.

### The Mountain Diagrammed (Mandala Theology)

The Buddhist and Hindu maṇḍala is Meru flattened into a ​map: the square’s four gates are its faces, the inner palace the summit’s city, the concentric rings its seven world-encircling ranges. To construct a mandala is to rebuild Meru; ‌to enter it is to climb. The Vajrayāna made the diagram the path itself.

### The Churning’s Spindle (Samudra Manthana)

When the gods and demons churned the ocean of milk, ​the churning-rod was Mandara, Meru’s little brother of a mountain; the serpent Vāsuki the rope. Meru’s family thus supplied the axis of the gods’ greatest work — the axis-mountain’s ​line, lending itself to every cosmic rotation.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Meru concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about ‌the name:

- **The Axis** — The world turns on Meru; the pole star wheels above its summit as the heavens’ nail-head.
- **The Four Faces** — Gold to the east, ‌crystal south, ruby west, lapis north — the four colours of the mandala.
- **City of the Gods** — Indra’s Amarāvatī crowns the summit; the thirty-three gods feast in its ‌halls.
- **The Mandala’s Map** — Every maṇḍala diagrams Meru: centre, four gates, and the enclosing world-rings.

Meru’s monuments are every stupa and ​pagoda — the Borobudur terraces walk the pilgrim up Sumeru; the temple mountains of Angkor are Meru in sandstone. The maṇḍala-paintings of Tibet diagram it ten thousand times.

## Across Cultures

Meru is shared property: Hindu Meru, Buddhist Sumeru, ​Jain Meru of the madhyaloka. The Greeks of Bactria heard Olympus in it; and the East Asian Buddhist cosmologies drew Sumeru as the world’s spike on temple banners from ‌Java to Japan. The mountain out-religioned every religion that mapped it.

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[aditi|Aditi]], [[agni|Agni]], [[ambika|Ambikā]], [[amsa|Aṃśa]], [[arjuna|Arjuna]], and ​[[bhakti|Bhakti]].

## Cultural Legacy

Every mandala, stupa, and temple plan is a Meru; the prayer-wheel’s axis and the pagoda’s spire are its hardware. ‘Sumeru’ and ‘Meru’ entered the names of ‌a thousand monasteries and mountains — and travellers to the real Himalaya argued for centuries which peak the geographers had meant.
